extracted.intended_audience: electric cooperative leaders, policymakers, regulators, and energy-sector stakeholders
extracted.subtask_short: commenting on EPA power plant rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria—expressed through NRECA reporting and statements—about how federal energy and environmental rules (especially EPA power plant, coal ash, and related rules) should be judged, designed, and litigated with respect to grid reliability, cost, statutory authority, and practical achievability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize regional flexibility, transparency, and fair cost-allocation for transmission projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow states, self-regulating entities such as co-ops, and other relevant authorities to prioritize regional flexibility, transparency and fair cost-allocation methodologies for new projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC and states should work together to ease transmission constraints and allow regional stakeholders to set priorities and cost-allocation approaches that reflect local needs and fairness concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission planning focused on load-serving entities and consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: “FERC should focus transmission planning and expansion on meeting the needs of [load-serving entities] and the consumers they serve.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transmission planning and expansion decisions should be driven by the needs of load-serving entities (LSEs) and their customers rather than other abstract system metrics; plans should reflect the practical needs of end users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance cost and reliability; consider consumer affordability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any solution to meet growing energy and transmission demand must consider the costs to consumers and strike a balance between cost and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators and policymakers should weigh consumer bill impacts when crafting rules or approving projects; policies that enhance reliability but impose unaffordable costs may be unacceptable, especially for consumer-owned co-ops serving persistently poor counties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation of cooperatives to provide safe, reliable, affordable service
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperatives share an obligation to serve their members by providing safe, reliable and affordable electric service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and regulatory decisions affecting co-ops should respect their duty to members and not impose requirements that undermine that obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandated technologies must be adequately demonstrated and achievable
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA’s rule relies on the use of inadequately demonstrated carbon capture and storage technology and unrealistic compliance timelines, making the standards unlawful and unachievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before mandating technology-based standards, agencies should rely on technologies that have been demonstrated at the necessary scale; otherwise, rules impose infeasible obligations and risk premature retirements of generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory timelines must reflect real-world lead times
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule’s timelines are too tight given long lead times for necessary upgrades (example: electrostatic precipitator alterations can take three years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should set compliance schedules that account for long procurement and construction lead times for major plant upgrades; failure to do so can force shutdowns or impose unrecoverable costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider grid adequacy and reliability in rulemaking (statutory duty under Clean Air Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must adequately consider the grid’s overall 'energy requirements' and reliability impacts when deciding the best system of emission reduction; failing to do so violates the Clean Air Act's directive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemakings that could prompt premature retirements or loss of reliability services should include thorough analyses of grid adequacy and explain how the rule addresses those concerns; agencies should respond to operator recommendations (e.g., 'safety valve' options) or justify why they are not adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reliability attributes beyond energy (spinning reserves, frequency response, voltage support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of coal plants can remove services such as spinning reserves, frequency response and voltage support that are critical to reliability—rules must consider replacing those services, not just energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating retirements or resource transitions, planners and rulewriters should require or ensure mechanisms to replace ancillary and stability services that retiring plants provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include and consider safety-valve or mitigation options offered by grid operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Grid operators offered several 'safety valve' options to mitigate reliability concerns before the rule was finalized; the final rule did not address these recommendations or explain why it rejected them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should engage with grid operators' proposed mitigation measures, document responses, and where appropriate adopt or explain rejection of operator-proposed safeguards to avoid unmitigated reliability risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use risk-based, state-plan approaches rather than one-size-fits-all rules for legacy coal ash
rubrics_metrics.description: The legacy coal ash rule applies a monolithic approach and broad, unclear definitions to already-closed sites rather than setting up a risk-based federal CCR permitting program and approving state plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer targeted, risk-based regulation and state implementation plans to avoid imposing unnecessary duplicative costs on already-closed sites or upending beneficial uses; clarify definitions to avoid unexpectedly expanding regulated units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve beneficial uses and avoid expanding regulation to exempt uses
rubrics_metrics.description: The new rule could expose currently exempt beneficial uses of CCR to stringent requirements because EPA underestimated the number of CCR management units under its vague definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule language should protect legitimate beneficial uses (e.g., use of CCR in concrete) and avoid vague definitions that broaden the regulated universe beyond agency intent and stakeholder expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure access to public lands and protect utility rights-of-way for grid expansion/hardening
rubrics_metrics.description: BLM’s Conservation and Landscape Health Rule could curtail co-ops’ ability to access public lands for transmission, distribution, vegetation management and maintenance by elevating conservation as a priority use and expanding 'areas of critical environmental concern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Land-management rules should preserve timely and prioritized processes for utility rights-of-way, wildfire mitigation, and grid hardening to avoid jeopardizing reliability and safety in rural areas; avoid creating leasing or designation processes that enable third parties to block critical energy projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing irreversible or unrecoverable costs on utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-ops could be forced to spend 'exorbitant' sums to comply with standards that may later be deemed unlawful; those costs are unrecoverable even if a rule is vacated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should consider the financial consequences of requiring major capital investments and weigh the risk of imposing sunk costs on utilities, especially when legal challenges to the rule are foreseeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules must be within statutory authority and supported by the agency's findings
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA acted unlawfully by tightening standards despite finding no residual health risks or identifying new cost-effective technologies that would warrant tighter standards; agencies must not exceed their statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules should be grounded in statutory mandates, supported by record evidence (e.g., demonstrable benefits or necessary findings), and avoid arbitrary expansions of regulatory reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy decisions should be anchored by core principles: reliability, resilience, security, affordability
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE official: four principles should anchor what DOE and co-ops do—reliability, resilience, security and affordability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or evaluating policy, regulators, utilities and stakeholders should test proposals against these four principles and prioritize solutions that reasonably balance them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor cross-sector collaboration and upfront stakeholder engagement over litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-sector cooperation and early collaboration among DOE, NRECA and other stakeholders produced a successful outcome on transformer standards; upfront collaboration is preferable to later litigation or adversarial regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should seek early, meaningful stakeholder engagement to craft practical, implementable policies; where possible, negotiate solutions that reduce the need for litigation and regulatory reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for rapid demand growth (AI, data centers, electrification) and align permitting/supply lead times
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid increases in power demand from data centers and electrification create urgency; developers can build faster than long lead times for utility equipment allow, so planning must anticipate accelerated demand while considering resource availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planning and permitting regimes should account for accelerated demand growth and mismatched timelines between customer-side builds and utility infrastructure procurement; consider options to accelerate transmission/substation construction or interim supply solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'one-size-fits-all' approaches that create disproportionate burdens on specific operators or regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform federal requirements (e.g., for inactive coal ash impoundments) can impose unnecessary and duplicative costs on cooperatives and disrupt plant operations where state rules already provided closure or mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules with flexibility or carve-outs where warranted by local conditions, prior remediation, or differing fuel/technology characteristics to prevent undue burdens on particular regions or facility types.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a rule poses imminent, substantial harm, pursue expedited judicial relief (stay/remand)
rubrics_metrics.description: NRECA urged quick judicial review and requested stays of EPA rules on the grounds they pose 'substantial, irreparable, and immediate harm' to electric co-ops and grid reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In advocacy and litigation strategy, demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits and irreparable harm to justify expedited court action or stays when regulations would cause immediate reliability or financial crises.
